headline: A 2018 Senate resolution that would have blocked a federal rule extending how long short-term health insurance plans can last.
what_it_does: This joint resolution would have canceled a 2018 rule from the Treasury, Labor, and Health and Human Services departments. The rule allowed short-term, limited-duration health insurance plans to run for an initial period of less than 12 months, with a total of up to 36 months including renewals. Before the rule, these plans were limited to less than 3 months including renewals. These plans are exempt from some Affordable Care Act market rules, such as the requirement to cover preexisting conditions.

who_it_affects.group: People who buy health insurance on their own
who_it_affects.how: They would have been unable to buy short-term plans lasting up to 36 months, so they would have kept the shorter 3-month limit.

who_it_affects.group: Insurance companies that sell short-term plans
who_it_affects.how: They would have been barred from offering the longer-duration short-term plans that the rule allowed.

who_it_affects.group: People with preexisting conditions who shop for short-term plans
who_it_affects.how: They would have kept the stronger Affordable Care Act protections instead of facing the longer-term plans, which are not required to cover preexisting conditions.
